analysis.one_liner: Lets a second generic drug maker launch when the first generic approved stalls and never starts selling.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee with no cosponsors and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Right now, the first generic company to challenge a brand-name drug gets 180 days of exclusive sales once it starts marketing — a reward meant to encourage generic competition. But that system can stall: a first filer can get approved and then delay launching, keeping every other generic off the market and prices high. This bill would let the FDA approve a waiting second generic maker once the first applicant's case has been pending at least 33 months, the first filer is not blocked by a patent lawsuit, and the second company certifies it can start selling within 75 days. If the second company fails to launch within 75 days, it loses its approval. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who need drugs stuck in the exclusivity queue: when a generic company wins approval but sits on it, prices stay at brand-name levels for everyone. By letting a ready second generic maker launch, the bill would speed up competition and lower prices. Taxpayers and employers who help pay for medicines also benefit indirectly.

how_it_helps.text: It allows the FDA to approve a waiting second generic maker once a first applicant has had an application pending for at least 33 months and still has not launched, cutting off a strategy of parking exclusivity to keep competition out.

It imposes a forfeiture rule: a subsequent applicant approved under this pathway must start selling within 75 days or lose effective approval, so the new approval actually results in a drug on pharmacy shelves rather than another parked license.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers, which would face generic competition sooner, and first-filing generic companies, which could lose exclusive sales windows they had banked on when they sit on an approved drug instead of launching it.

drawbacks.text: It trims the 180-day exclusivity reward that is the main financial incentive for generic companies to challenge brand-name patents; weakening it could lead fewer companies to file challenges, which over time could mean fewer low-cost generics reaching the market.
It adds conditions and certifications (a 75-day marketing commitment with a cure process and forfeiture rules) that create new administrative complexity for FDA and for generic applicants.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is cheaper generic drugs for consumers; the cost falls almost entirely on brand-name companies and first-filing generic makers that would lose some control over the 180-day exclusivity reward. The conditions (33-month wait, certification of readiness, forfeiture for not launching) are designed to prevent generic makers from hoarding approvals without launching, which addresses the main good-faith objection — that the change could undermine the exclusivity incentive that persuades generic firms to challenge brand-name patents in the first place.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never advanced further before the session's end.

narrative.text: Rep. Budzinski introduced the bill on February 6, 2025.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which controls most drug-pricing legislation.
It attracted no cosponsors and no further action appears in its record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers and any generic company relying on the first-filer exclusivity rules keep the status quo, including the ability to shelve a generic approval without launching it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers and the status quo

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan pattern ever took shape.

industries.industry: Generic drug makers (other than the exclusivity holder)
industries.note: A waiting second generic applicant can now get approved and launch after 33 months if the first filer has not marketed the drug, opening a market previously blocked by one company's exclusivity. Consumers benefit from the added competition.
Companies that file first but sit on their approval without launching would lose the ability to keep all rivals off the market indefinitely, weakening a lever they can use to keep prices high.
Faster generic entry ends the price premium brand-name companies charge while a generic launch is stalled, reducing revenue from older drugs.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has no cosponsors and no committee action a year into the Congress; the overwhelmingly likely path is that it dies quietly in committee like most drug-pricing bills introduced without leadership backing, though similar generic-competition provisions have occasionally been attached to larger packages.
